newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-UK interest rates unchanged, output fragile.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-UK interest rates unchanged, output fragile.

text.p: The Bank of England made clear on Thursday that interest rates had been left unchanged at six percent as official figures showed manufacturing output was enjoying only a fragile recovery.

The central bank made no formal statement on monetary policy but it conducted money market operations at established dealing rates, providing definitive evidence that finance minister Kenneth Clarke had ordered no change in rates on Wednesday.

Clarke, the Chancellor of the Exchequer, held his monthly monetary meeting with Bank of England Governor Eddie George on Wednesday. There had been a lingering suspicion on financial markets that a rate rise might be announced on Thursday.
George, who fears a resurgence in inflation in the next 18 months, has been pressing for higher rates since December.
But Clarke is anxious to avoid tightening monetary policy in the run-up to the looming election as this would mean dearer home loans for millions of Britons.

Economists said December industrial production figures, which both men would have been aware of at their meeting on Wednesday, strengthened the Chancellor's argument that there was little immediate risk of the economy overheating.

Manufacturing output grew just 0.2 percent in December from the previous month after an unexpected 0.3 percent fall in November. The annual rate of growth accelerated to 1.4 percent from 0.5 percent in November.
Overall industrial production rose 0.6 percent in December and was up 1.9 percent year-on-year.

Angela Knight, economic secretary to the Treasury, said the figures showed "the wheels and cogs of manufacturing turning faster" in the second half of 1996. "Recent business surveys show higher production on the way in 1997," she said.
Economists said total industrial production was slightly stronger than expected in December, largely due to sharp rises in energy output because of unusually cold weather.
There was also robust growth in durable goods production, reflecting strong demand in the consumer sector.
"Overall, these figures provide confirmation that, while the manufacturing recovery remains on track, it is still fragile," said Jonathan Loynes, an economist at HSBC Markets.
Simon Briscoe, an economist at Nikko Europe, said the weakness in manufacturing was a strong argument for a stable monetary policy.
"We believe that the fragile state of the manufacturing sector probably provides enough ammunition for the Chancellor to keep interest rates on hold until after the election," he said.
An election must be held by May 22.
A leading business survey showed high street sales picked up in January and exceeded retailers' expectations.

The Confederation of British Industry (CBI) said 53 percent of retailers reported higher sales volumes compared with January 1996, while only 17 percent reported lower turnover, giving a positive balance of 36 percent.

"Retailers did better in terms of January's sales growth than they had expected as consumers were confident enough to step up their spending," said Alastair Eperon, chairman of the CBI's Distributive Trade Survey panel.
"However, the rate of underlying sales growth eased for the second consecutive month, although the increase in trade remains robust."
